title: Core Web Vitals explained simply: LCP, INP and CLS

content.imageAlt: Laptop showing a dashboard of page load time statistics
content.excerpt: Three acronyms Google uses to judge your visitors’ experience. What they measure, the scores you need and why red ones cost you customers.
content.lead: LCP, INP and CLS sound like tech jargon, but they measure three things anyone notices when they open a website: **how long it takes to appear**, **how quickly it responds** and **how much it jumps around while loading**. Google calls them Core Web Vitals and uses them to assess visitor experience. Let’s go through them one by one, no jargon.
content.text:
## What Core Web Vitals are

They’re three measurements Google picked to describe the real experience of people visiting a page. The key word is **real**: Google collects this data (anonymously) from the Chrome browsers of people who actually visit your website, not from a lab test.

For each metric Google sets three bands: *good*, *needs improvement* and *poor*. A page passes when at least 75% of visits fall into the “good” band.

## LCP: how long it takes to appear

**Largest Contentful Paint** measures how long it takes for the largest element in the visible part of the page to appear: usually a hero image or a big heading. It’s the moment the visitor thinks “OK, the page is here”.

- **Good**: within 2.5 seconds.
- **Needs improvement**: between 2.5 and 4 seconds.
- **Poor**: over 4 seconds.

The usual culprits behind a slow LCP are oversized images, a slow server and too many files blocking the page from displaying.

## INP: how quickly it responds

**Interaction to Next Paint** measures the time between a visitor’s action (a tap, a click, a key press) and the page’s visible response. Since March 2024 it has replaced the old FID metric, because it reflects real responsiveness far better.

- **Good**: within 200 milliseconds.
- **Needs improvement**: between 200 and 500 milliseconds.
- **Poor**: over 500 milliseconds.

With a high INP, the visitor taps a button and “nothing happens”: they tap again, get impatient and leave. The culprit is almost always too much JavaScript, often from plugins or third-party services.

## CLS: how much the page jumps around

**Cumulative Layout Shift** measures how much the elements on the page move while it loads. You know when you’re about to tap a link and a banner suddenly appears and pushes it down? That.

- **Good**: below 0.1.
- **Needs improvement**: between 0.1 and 0.25.
- **Poor**: over 0.25.

The fix is almost always to reserve the right space for images, videos and banners before they load, and to load fonts so the text doesn’t change size.

## Lighthouse vs real-world data: what’s the difference?

When you test a website with PageSpeed Insights you get two different things. At the top, if the site has enough traffic, you’ll see **real-world data** from the last 28 days: that’s what Google uses. Below it is the **Lighthouse** test, a simulation run there and then on a mid-range phone.

Lighthouse is great for finding problems and checking an improvement straight away. Real-world data, on the other hand, updates slowly: after a fix it takes a few weeks to see it change.

## Why they matter for your business

Core Web Vitals are among the signals Google uses to judge the experience a page offers. They won’t get you to the top on their own, but with comparable content a fast website has the edge.

Above all, they matter to people: a website that opens quickly, responds instantly and doesn’t jump around builds trust. A slow one drives customers away before they’ve even read what you offer.

## How to measure them in 5 minutes

1. Open **PageSpeed Insights** and enter your website’s address.
2. Look at the **Mobile** tab first: it’s the strictest and the most important.
3. Check whether the three scores are green, orange or red.
4. Repeat the test on your key pages, not just the homepage.
5. If you have Search Console, open the **Core Web Vitals** report to see which groups of pages have problems.

If you see red, don’t panic: in most cases there’s a lot you can improve without rebuilding the website.
